Direct answer | “Geodetic surveyors” on this page correspond to U.S. SOC 17-1022.01. Work falls into several categories: (I) control-network and datum design—plan or direct surveys according to project and regional datum requirements, establishing control networks and observation plans, including point locations, strength of geometry, accuracy criteria and check conditions; (II) field observations—survey large areas of the Earth's surface using satellite observations, GNSS, LIDAR or related methods, performing static/dynamic observations, connected leveling, traverses, triangulation and trilateration; (III) calculations and adjustment—calculate precise horizontal and vertical positions of surface points, compute control-network coordinates and elevations using direct leveling or other geodetic techniques, and perform adjustment and accuracy/deviation analysis; (IV) data/database maintenance—maintain databases of geodetic and related information, including coordinate, descriptive and quality-assurance data, and verify the mathematical correctness of new data; (V) quality/compliance review—analyze control or survey data for compliance with project specifications or land surveying standards, assess control-data quality and determine whether additional survey data are required, requesting more when field collection errors occur or specifications are not met; (VI) deliverable submission/collaboration—provide compiled geodetic data to government agencies or the public, work with engineering, construction and geographic information teams, and maintain deliverables, metadata and survey point descriptions. The work cycle connects task/datum confirmation—control-network and observation design—field observations/checks—calculations, adjustment and quality assessment—deliverables, databases and metadata—submission, review and additional observations. This page does not conflate this occupation with adjacent land surveyors, cartographers/photogrammetrists, geographic information technicians, civil engineers or data scientists. Tasks may involve land grids and boundary surveys; appropriately licensed practitioners may certify legal survey documents under the relevant jurisdiction. The classification title itself grants no judicial title-determination, structural-design or competent-authority approval powers.

O*NET and BLS profile highlights | This page corresponds to U.S. SOC 17-1022.01, “Geodetic Surveyors” (architecture and engineering occupations; O*NET updated in 2026). Official scope: measure large areas of the Earth's surface using satellite observations, GNSS, LIDAR or related methods. O*NET core tasks include analyzing control or survey data for compliance with project specifications or land surveying standards (importance 91); surveying precise surface-point positions, elevations, alignments, areas, volumes, contours or other features (88); calculating precise horizontal and vertical positions of surface points (88); maintaining geodetic and related databases, including coordinate, descriptive and quality-assurance data (88); verifying the mathematical correctness of newly collected survey data (86); computing horizontal and vertical control-network coordinates using geodetic techniques such as direct leveling, triangulation, trilateration and traversing (83); planning or directing geodetic personnel and providing technical advice as needed (81); assessing control-data quality to determine whether engineering, construction or other projects need additional survey data (80); providing compiled geodetic data to government agencies or the public (76); and requesting additional survey data when field collection errors occur or engineering survey specifications are not met (76). The most important work activities are working with computers (91), processing information (90), analyzing data/information (87), getting information (87), and documenting/recording information (83). Wage and employment scope note: data displayed by O*NET under this occupation (17-1022.01) are labelled as covering broader occupational group 17-1022, “Surveyors”, without separate reporting for this exact occupation. This page labels that scope faithfully and does not invent precise figures.

Do not make unauthorized judgments or commitments on matters beyond your qualifications or authorization, such as ownership/legal boundary conclusions, engineering acceptance or classified-deliverable approvals. Occupational definition | Geodetic surveyors on this page correspond to U.S. SOC 17-1022.01, “Geodetic Surveyors”. Official scope: measure large areas of the Earth's surface using satellite observations, GNSS, LIDAR or related methods. Core tasks include analyzing control/survey data for compliance with project specifications or land surveying standards; surveying precise surface-point locations, elevations, alignments, areas, volumes, contours or other features; calculating precise horizontal/vertical positions of surface points; maintaining databases of geodetic and related information, including coordinate, descriptive and quality-assurance data; verifying the mathematical correctness of newly collected survey data; computing horizontal/vertical control-network coordinates using direct leveling, triangulation, trilateration or traversing; planning/directing survey personnel and assessing control-data quality to determine whether additional observations are needed; and providing compiled geodetic data to government agencies or the public. Outputs include control results, coordinates, elevations, databases and quality descriptions. What personality is better suited to geodetic surveying? This occupation places more emphasis on accuracy and awareness of standards, endurance and organization across field and office work, rigor with data and checking, and willingness to take responsibility for deliverables and data security than on any personality type. O*NET's interest code is RIC (Realistic–Investigative–Conventional), and its work styles emphasize attention to detail and dependability; these can be starting points for exploration.

Are introverts suited to this occupation? Yes. The occupation involves extensive independent data processing and calculations, alongside communication with project teams, design and construction teams, geographic information teams and clients (email 93% daily, telephone 54% daily, and 58% reporting face-to-face or individual and team discussions weekly or more often).
Extraversion does not determine work performance. Check clear expression, anomaly reporting and checking habits against tasks; do not present extraversion as a proven collaboration advantage.

Which MBTI type is best for this occupation? No type has been proven best. MBTI is not a professional qualification or ability assessment tool; occupational adaptation mainly depends on awareness of accuracy, adherence to standards, instrument and software skills, and deliverable management skills.

Which Holland interest types are better suited to this occupation? O*NET's interest code is RIC: Realistic (fieldwork, instruments and hands-on engineering), Investigative (analyzing and investigating spatial and data problems), and Conventional (organizing information and records according to standards). Use it to explore task preferences, not predict performance.

This page has not established validation of personality or interest scores for individual performance in this occupation; they can only support self-questioning. Lawful practice and professional assessments follow actual requirements, while simulated exercises only provide learning observations.

Can I do this occupation if I am weak at mathematics? It requires quantitative abilities in geometry, coordinates, errors and adjustment, with extensive numerical calculations and checks in daily work. Quantitative foundations can be improved through training, but a complete inability to adapt to numerical and data work is a significant limitation.

Does this occupation require high emotional intelligence? It requires emotional stability, patience and collaboration with multiple parties, but no particular assessment score. Fieldwork, schedule pressure and rework require self-regulation and reporting according to standards.

Can the Enneagram determine whether I am suited to it? No. The Enneagram is a self-exploration tool, not a conclusion about occupational ability or fit. Assess fit by whether you can complete observations, adjustments, deliverables and checks under qualification and standards requirements.

Use the complete G1 materials, three tables and answers to observe your calculation, version quality-control and handover habits in this exercise. Do not judge long-term fit from one exercise; verify real fieldwork and licensing separately.

Signs of fit: willingness to take responsibility for observations, calculations and deliverables within qualifications, standards and authorization; ability to work rigorously with spatial reference systems and numerical calculations over the long term; and ability to maintain checks and records under fieldwork and schedule pressure, reporting exceedances or anomalies according to procedures.

Reasons for caution: difficulty working over the long term under extremely demanding accuracy, standards and checking requirements; difficulty accepting the effects of field conditions, seasons and travel; or unwillingness to report and hand over according to procedures when qualifications or authorization are exceeded.

Validation suggestion: first use a simulated or real surveying task to test datum confirmation, plan design, observations, adjustment, deliverable submission and checking. paragraphs: Boundary | The following are failure scenarios inferred from tasks and editorial control suggestions; risk frequencies have not been measured. Issue deliverables according to the actual jurisdiction, organizational qualifications, personnel conditions, project authorization and applicable standards. Surveying tasks and lawful boundary work may overlap; an occupational title neither grants nor excludes specific authority. Hand over legal matters, engineering acceptance or state-secret matters beyond your authorization to the appropriate roles and authorities.

Risk examples include inconsistent datums, missed gross errors, concealed overwriting of records, providing materials without authority, and field environmental hazards. This is not a ranking of risk frequencies; pause the relevant stage and obtain supporting evidence when tolerances are exceeded, information is missing or authorization is unclear. Check Chinese organizational qualifications, personnel practice conditions and work credentials separately. You, quality and project roles; projects, clients, engineering and ownership

Misjudging the coordinate system, projection zone, elevation datum or epoch, or failing to identify unstable known points, gross errors or systematic bias, may cause systematic errors in deliverables and lead to engineering rework, ownership issues or safety problems.

Before the task, check datums, projections, epochs and known-point stability and record the basis. Conduct observations and adjustment according to tolerances and checking requirements, with repeat observations and closure-error checks. Immediately pause, review and take supplementary measurements when datums are inconsistent, gross errors occur or tolerances are exceeded.
Scenario | Known points supplied for a project have systematic discrepancies with existing deliverables. The schedule is tight, and the client wants deliverables issued first and checked later.
You, quality and qualification roles; organizations, projects and the public

Missing or fabricated original observations, concealed overwriting, or inconsistent versions may obstruct quality traceability. Lawful factual corrections must retain original values, supporting grounds, actual times and personnel; not every later correction is a violation.

Retain original materials and versions, and list missing items as awaiting supporting evidence. When adding factual records or making corrections, state actual times, old and new values, grounds and responsible persons; do not backdate, overwrite or report selectively.

Scenario | At handover, the previous shift's original observation data lack antenna heights and observation-period records, and the adjustment deliverables and drawings have inconsistent versions. You are advised to fill the gaps using a template.
You, confidentiality and information roles; organizations, clients and competent authorities

Providing state-secret or controlled materials without authority may cause disclosure, contractual or legal consequences. First check classification, intended use and recipient; apply the respective rules to ordinary public information, personal information and state secrets.

Check Chinese organizational qualifications, personnel practice conditions and work credentials separately. External provision of state-secret deliverables and publication of important geographic information data follow Articles 34/37 of the Surveying and Mapping Law respectively; ordinary sharing does not universally require administrative approval. First check actual authorization and intended use for controlled materials. Immediately report suspected unauthorized conduct through procedures and retain facts and records.
Scenario | A stakeholder requests that state-secret or controlled surveying and mapping deliverables and control-point coordinates be sent in an uncontrolled group chat for quick coordination.
You, qualification and legal roles; organizations, clients and professional practice

Issuing surveying and mapping deliverables beyond qualifications or authorization, making ownership or legal boundary conclusions, or substituting for engineering acceptance conclusions may incur administrative and legal liability and professional practice risks.

Issue deliverables within qualifications, authorization and project scope. Hand over ownership, legal, engineering acceptance and state-secret approval matters to appropriately qualified roles or organizations. When asked to exceed qualifications or authorization, first explain the boundary and hand over according to procedures.
Scenario | During a staff shortage, you are asked to issue ownership-related survey deliverables or engineering acceptance conclusions beyond your organization's qualifications and authorization.
You, field teams and equipment roles; project progress and personnel safety

When one person handles critical fieldwork or data processing, leave, equipment failure, weather or seasonal effects may interrupt operations and deliverables, delaying projects and affecting quality and safety.

Establish backup and handover rules for fieldwork, data, equipment and personnel. Keep critical methods, parameters and deliverable versions reproducible and recorded. Report staffing or equipment shortages according to procedures and adjust priorities; do not undertake fieldwork with unresolved hazards.

Scenario | The only colleague familiar with a particular datum transformation and adjustment process is on leave. The project requires that colleague to guide untrained staff by telephone to process and submit deliverables temporarily.
You, outsourcing providers and technical service platforms; projects, deliverables and data security

Unclear delivery and acceptance arrangements for outsourced observations, data processing, equipment or technical services, or unclear ownership of deliverables, data and metadata or rules for fee changes, may cause rework, fee disputes and unclear quality and data-security responsibilities.

For outsourcing and technical cooperation, clearly define and record scope, standards, acceptance, data and deliverable ownership, and fee-change rules. Review and accept delivered results. Pause, review and report disputes about delivery, acceptance or ownership.

Scenario | After completing observations, an outsourcing provider requests payment without submitting original data or checking records. On site, you are asked to sign off first, with data and review to follow later.

values: M1 | G1-v1 fictional local elevation closure loop A→B→C→A; starting elevation at A: 100.000m, using a local teaching datum with no national datum, epoch or projection definition. Do not perform transformations or formal surveying and mapping. The exercise allows |closure error|≤8mm; this is not a real survey-grade tolerance. If exceeded, do not adjust results or judge formal deliverables as acceptable.

M2 | Three original elevation differences: AB+1.234m, BC−0.456m, CA−0.768m; lengths 0.4/0.3/0.3km are only for totaling. Accumulate in order to obtain unadjusted elevations at B, C and the return to A. Closure error = return elevation at A − starting elevation at A; retain signs and units.

M3 | Metadata v1: instrument checking and calibration evidence, repeat observations and known-point stability confirmation are all blank. Record each as UNKNOWN, not FAIL or PASS; do not fabricate field records. The exercise supplies no error model or weights, so do not calculate an adjustment.

M4 | Deliverable v2 awaiting verification claims closure error 1mm/PASS and elevation at B 101.243m. Compare these with independent calculations from M2, listing original values, correct values, differences and causes awaiting investigation. Differences alone cannot establish who changed values or the specific source of a gross error.

M5 | Submitted to quality lead Q for review on month 10, day 1, at 14:00; status remains unconfirmed at 14:04. The exercise requires escalation to lead T before 14:20. External requester U asks for real control points, with no data-classification or authorization materials. Q/T are fictional; do not actually send anything. Record 4 minutes elapsed and 16 minutes until the deadline, retain the unconfirmed status, and refuse to guess entries or provide real materials.

M6 | Create three paper tables: calculation table (original data/formula/unit/result/exercise limit/status), discrepancy quality-control table (M number/version/discrepancy/UNKNOWN/request for supporting evidence), and handover draft (issue/request/responsible role/actual entry time/deadline/confirmation status). A pen or calculator suffices; no software, expert or fieldwork is required.
60 minutes: 15 minutes to read M1–M6, 15 minutes for calculations, 20 minutes for quality control and drafts, and 10 minutes for self-checking; paper practice only.

M4 understates the closure error by 9mm, reporting 1/10 of the correct value, and overstates B's elevation by 9mm. M3's three UNKNOWN items still await supporting evidence. Record M5's tolerance exceedance and unauthorized request separately; do not mark handling complete while unconfirmed. Completing the three tables suffices; there is no need to guess two errors that have occurred or provide a formal signature and seal.

entries.answer: This page's geodetic surveyors correspond to U.S. SOC 17-1022.01: surveying large areas of the Earth's surface using satellite observations, global navigation satellite systems (GNSS), light detection and ranging (LIDAR), or related methods. Core work includes analyzing control or survey data to ensure compliance with project specifications or land survey standards; conducting surveys to determine exact positions of surface points and measure positions, elevations, lines, areas, volumes, contours or other features; calculating precise horizontal and vertical positions of points on the Earth's surface; maintaining geodetic and related information databases, including coordinate, descriptive and quality-assurance data; verifying the mathematical correctness of newly collected survey data; calculating horizontal and vertical control-network coordinates using direct leveling, triangulation, trilateration or traverse techniques; planning or directing surveying staff and evaluating control data quality to determine whether additional observations are needed; and providing compiled geodetic data to government agencies or the public. Common employers include professional, scientific and technical services and other industries including construction and government. This page describes the U.S. occupational classification.

entries.answer: Core differences concern scale, accuracy and levels of authorization. This occupation works with large-area Earth reference frameworks, high-accuracy control networks, datum transformations, coordinates and elevations, producing control deliverables, coordinates, elevations, databases and quality explanations. Surveyors (17-1022.00) mainly survey parcels, ownership and engineering projects; cartographers and photogrammetrists (17-1021.00) focus on maps, imagery, photogrammetry and geographic visualization; geographic information technicians focus on spatial data management, analysis, mapping and systems; civil engineers (17-2051.00) focus on engineering structural design, construction and acceptance; and data scientists (15-2051.00) focus on statistics, machine learning and data modeling. Scales and authorization levels differ; authority to make ownership conclusions, perform engineering acceptance or approve state-secret deliverables cannot be carried across roles.

subject.name: Geodetic surveyors
subject.summary: Geodetic surveyors correspond to U.S. O*NET/SOC 17-1022.01, “Geodetic Surveyors”: they measure large areas of the Earth's surface using satellite observations, global navigation satellite systems (GNSS), light detection and ranging (LIDAR), or related methods. Core work includes analyzing control or survey data to ensure compliance with project specifications or land surveying standards; conducting surveys to determine precise locations of surface points and measure positions, elevations, alignments, areas, volumes, contours or other features; calculating precise horizontal and vertical positions of points on the Earth's surface; maintaining databases of geodetic and related information, including coordinate, descriptive and quality-assurance data; verifying the mathematical correctness of newly collected survey data; computing horizontal and vertical control-network coordinates using direct leveling, triangulation, trilateration or traverse techniques; planning or directing survey personnel and assessing control-data quality to determine whether additional observations are needed; and providing compiled geodetic data to government agencies or the public. Official scope, in the original wording: Measure large areas of the Earth's surface using satellite observations, global navigation satellite systems (GNSS), light detection and ranging (LIDAR), or related sources. Wage and employment scope note: figures displayed by O*NET under this occupation are labelled as covering the broader occupational group 17-1022, “Surveyors”.
